manifest.prompt: a set of three custom bezier curves that are described as feeling "sticky and punchy", present them as loops
consumers: builder writing three custom bezier easing curves
how_to_read: 1. Read the head first: the first 33 lines hold manifest, essence and routing (Read limit=33, or jq '{manifest, essence, routing}' sticky-punchy-curves.metadump.json).
2. Pick the route for your job and run its jq: jq '<routing[i].jq>' sticky-punchy-curves.metadump.json
3. Also pull the anti-keywords and review prompts (checks) for your scope: jq '.anti_keywords, .checks' sticky-punchy-curves.metadump.json
4. Look up any term (lowercase): jq '.index["<term>"]' sticky-punchy-curves.metadump.json  -> hits give id + path; not_meant lists senses to avoid.
5. Grep works too: every entry is one line, so grep -n '<word>' sticky-punchy-curves.metadump.json returns whole entries.

essence.one_sentence: A curve reads as sticky or punchy by where its progress is spent along time and whether it overshoots, and each word has several readings that different curves can carry.
essence.summary: Sticky: progress is held, then released or settled into place. Punchy: an early attack, a short kick, or a hard stop.

formula.full: cubic-bezier(x1, y1, x2, y2) with x in 0 to 1 and y free; progress spent early or late sets the feel, a peak above 1 adds a kick, and a flat tail adds a settle
formula.essential: where progress is spent, and whether it overshoots

roles.x1, x2: when the motion happens, bounded so time runs forward
roles.y1, y2: how far progress travels and whether it passes the target
roles.end slope (1 - y2) / (1 - x2): how the motion lands: a grip, a settle or a hard stop

poles: grip: a slow first fifth holds the start back
snap: fast early progress launches the element
fast attack: most of the change lands in the first frames
clean settle: a quiet tail that stops without a swing past the target
kick: one shallow peak past the target that clears quickly
wobble: a deep or repeated swing past the target
hold: progress rests near the end for a visible tail
hard stop: progress flattens abruptly after most of the travel

ak-lingering-duration.instead: a loop short enough that the peak and the rest both show in one cycle

ak-wobble-overshoot.instead: a small kick past the target that settles back within a few frames

ak-one-curve-thrice.instead: three different control-point sets, each with its own shape

ak-loop-resets-before-settle.instead: a dwell long enough that the curve reaches its end value before the loop restarts

ak-floaty-drift.instead: a fast middle with a firm arrival into the target

c-set-of-cubic-beziers.text: Review whether each curve is written as a cubic bezier timing function with four control values, so the set can be dropped into a timing function.

test.spec: cubic-bezier(x1, y1, x2, y2) with four numbers per curve

c-time-runs-forward.text: Review whether the x values of every control point stay inside 0 to 1, so time runs forward on each curve.

test.spec: x1 and x2 within [0, 1] for all three curves

c-ends-at-one.text: Review whether each curve ends at progress 1 at time 1 when sampled from t = 0 to t = 1.

test.spec: y(t) at t = 1 equals 1 for each curve

c-named-reading.text: Review whether each curve names the sticky or punchy reading it serves, so a viewer can tell the three apart.

test.spec: each curve's label or caption names one reading of sticky or punchy

c-early-attack.text: Review whether a curve meant as punchy spends a large share of its progress in the first fifth of its duration.

test.spec: share of total progress reached by 20 percent of time

c-duration-ranges.text: Review whether each pass duration sits within the small UI ranges researched for its kind of motion.

test.spec: duration in ms against press 100 to 160, dropdown 150 to 250, modal 200 to 500

c-overshoot-peak.text: Review whether any overshoot peaks above 1 and returns to 1, and whether the peak size matches the kick or wobble reading chosen for it.

test.spec: maximum of y(t) over dense samples, compared with the chosen reading's band

c-kick-clears.text: Review whether a shallow overshoot clears within a few frames, and whether a deep or repeated swing reads as wobble.

test.spec: the loop returns to rest without a second swing

c-loop-forward-and-back.text: Review whether each loop plays its curve once forward and shows the reverse pass, so the full path is visible.

test.spec: loop plays forward then backward and the element returns to its start

c-overshoot-visible.text: Review whether a loop of an overshooting curve carries the element past its target and back, so the overshoot shows without numbers on screen.

test.spec: element passes the end mark and returns within the loop

c-track-reads-as-time.text: Review whether the moving element travels on a plain track, so timing reads as position over time.

test.spec: one element on an empty horizontal track per curve

c-keyword-reference.text: Review whether a named keyword curve such as ease-out or ease-in-out appears beside the set, so each custom bend shows against a familiar one.

test.spec: a reference curve appears in the presentation

request._about: The user's words, verbatim from the prompt. Nothing glossed.

u-set-of-three.term: set of three custom bezier curves
u-set-of-three.anchor: a set of three custom bezier curves
u-set-of-three.text: The deliverable is a set of three custom bezier curves.

u-sticky-punchy.text: The curves are described as feeling sticky and punchy. Both words are quality words and each needs readings.

u-as-loops.text: The curves are presented as loops.

task_discipline._about: Discipline rungs: motion and interaction design, and easing and timing theory. Principles as facets, each with how it plays out for a curve described as sticky or punchy. Options, not requirements: each 'implies' line is one reading, and the consumer chooses or combines them.

ds-entry-ease-out.text: Elements that enter the screen decelerate into their final position, so the eye catches a fast start and the element comes to rest softly.
behaviors: A dropdown that starts fast reads as responsive and then lands softly
An entry that starts slow reads as reluctant and holds the user waiting
ds-entry-ease-out.principle: An entering object arrives from motion, so it decelerates as it comes to rest.
signals: fast first frames
long soft tail before rest

implies.sticky: a slow arrival that eases into the target

ds-entry-ease-in-exit.text: Elements that leave the screen accelerate as they go, and the exit runs shorter than the matching entrance so the content clears quickly.
behaviors: An exit that starts slow lingers and makes the viewer wait for it to finish
A shorter exit clears the space before the next element arrives
ds-entry-ease-in-exit.principle: Leaving motion gains speed, because the viewer's attention has already moved on.
signals: slow start then quick departure
exit duration below entrance duration

implies.sticky: a release that gathers speed after a hold

ds-entry-ease-in-out-on-screen.text: Elements that move between two points and stay on screen usually take a symmetric curve, eased at both ends. Secondary guides cite this; no primary source was confirmed.
behaviors: A symmetric curve on a card that moves in place reads as deliberate and heavy
Using the same symmetric curve for both entry and exit makes one of them lag
A symmetric curve drops the fast attack that punchy readings rely on
ds-entry-ease-in-out-on-screen.principle: Movement that stays on screen has no arrival or departure, so both ends get easing.
signals: equal slow ends
midpoint with the highest speed

implies.sticky: a grip at the start and a slow hold at the end
implies.punchy: weaker, because the curve gives up the early attack

ds-entry-bezier-overshoot.text: A cubic-bezier with a control-point y value outside 0 to 1 passes the target and then returns to it, which is the mechanism behind overshoot. The x values stay inside 0 to 1.
behaviors: Raising the second control point's y above 1 makes the value pass the end state and return
Keeping x inside 0 to 1 keeps time moving forward through the curve
ds-entry-bezier-overshoot.principle: Progress may exceed its endpoints, but time cannot run backward.
signals: value above 1 mid-curve
a return to 1 near the end

implies.punchy: the overshoot itself is the kick
implies.sticky: a return to rest after the overshoot reads as a hold

ds-entry-overshoot-size.text: Aggressive overshoot adds a bounce to drawers and modals. A small overshoot reads as a snap or kick. The line between them is a judgement, not a number.
behaviors: A brief, shallow overshoot on a press reads as a kick and clears fast
A deep overshoot on a drawer or modal reads as a bounce that draws attention to itself
A long overshoot that keeps swinging reads as a wobble, not a snap
ds-entry-overshoot-size.principle: Overshoot is a signal of force; more of it reads as more weight, until it reads as play.
signals: overshoot shallow enough to clear in a few frames
repeated swings after the target

tokens.overshoot_share_of_travel: a few percent for a kick, larger for a bounce

implies.punchy: a shallow overshoot that clears quickly
implies.sticky: an overshoot that returns and holds, with no further swing

ds-entry-velocity-settle.text: Most of an ease-out's visible motion happens early. The slow final stretch is where the viewer decides the motion is over, which is what reads as the settle.
behaviors: A curve that covers most of its distance early looks finished before its duration ends
A flat tail near the end makes the element seem to hold its value
ds-entry-velocity-settle.principle: Velocity carries the eye, and the settle is where the eye judges the motion complete.
signals: early speed peak
near-zero speed for the final fraction

implies.punchy: a high early peak followed by a short tail
implies.sticky: an early settle that holds near the end value

curve_mechanics._about: How control points produce motion (query log 3, 4, 5, 15, 16). Values from the research shards (cm-bezier-map, cm-constraints, cm-overshoot-numbers, cm-duration-ranges) are cited by id, not re-derived.

parameters._about: Numeric checks for a curve, with units and status.

p-end-progress.text: Three values to check a timing curve against: progress 1 at time 1, x values in 0 to 1, and y values free.

options._about: options, not requirements: overshoot amount and duration are open choices with tradeoffs. No option is chosen here.

opt-overshoot-amount.decision: how much overshoot the curve carries
opt-overshoot-amount.text: Overshoot is a choice between a clean landing and a visible kick, and each option trades something against the sticky and punchy readings.

options.option: no overshoot, y values inside 0 to 1
options.fits_when: the reading is a grip and release without a kick
options.tradeoff: calm and clean, but gives up the punch of a kick

options.fits_when: the punchy reading needs a visible kick and a short return
options.tradeoff: adds a visible kick; the return past the target adds time to the settle

options.option: snap, peak near 1.10 with a return to 1
options.fits_when: the bounce is the point of the motion, as on a press release
options.tradeoff: strongest punch; a viewer may read it as a wobble, and the longer return lengthens the motion

opt-duration.decision: how long one pass of the curve runs
opt-duration.text: Duration trades responsiveness against how much of the path a viewer can see in a loop.

options.fits_when: the curve stands for a press or release and should read as immediate
options.tradeoff: responsive, but a loop shows the path in a blink (cm-duration-ranges)

options.fits_when: the loop needs to show the whole path to a viewer
options.tradeoff: the path reads clearly, but past about 300 ms small UI starts to feel slow

options.fits_when: the three curves cover different distances
options.tradeoff: each curve feels proportionate, but the set is harder to compare side by side

cm-material-library.text: Material's utility easings split by screen movement: standard (0.2,0,0,1), standard decelerate (0,0,0,1) for entering, standard accelerate (0.3,0,1,1) for exiting, with emphasized variants for expressive motion.
behaviors: Decelerate tokens front-load movement for entering elements
Accelerate tokens back-load movement for exiting elements
The emphasized path is a multi-segment curve, not a single bezier
cm-material-library.principle: Easing follows the direction of travel on screen: enter, exit, or begin and end on screen.
signals: decelerate on entering panels
accelerate on dismissals

cm-ui-curve-families.text: A design-engineering skill summary recommends a strong ease-out (0.23,1,0.32,1) for UI interactions and a strong ease-in-out (0.77,0,0.175,1) for on-screen movement, and advises against ease-in for UI.
behaviors: A strong ease-out gives immediate movement on the first frame of the action
Ease-in delays the first visible movement, which is the moment a user watches most closely
cm-ui-curve-families.principle: The first moment of motion carries the feel of the response; curves that delay it read as lag.
signals: motion visible on the first frame
no long lead-in before movement
cm-ui-curve-families.open_questions_note: Summary of a third-party skill, not the author's own page; weaker than the spec or Material.

cm-duration-ranges.text: Common ranges: button press feedback 100 to 160 ms, tooltips 125 to 200 ms, dropdowns 150 to 250 ms, modals and drawers 200 to 500 ms; Material's short tokens run about 50 to 200 ms.
behaviors: Duration should grow with how far or how much area an element travels
A 100 to 160 ms press reads as immediate; past about 300 ms small UI starts to feel slow
cm-duration-ranges.principle: Duration tracks distance and the cost of waiting, so small controls stay short.
signals: under 300 ms for a control
a clear peak inside the first 200 ms

cm-css-loops.text: CSS loops with animation-iteration-count: infinite, animation-direction: alternate to play forward then back, and animation-delay to wait before the first iteration.
behaviors: alternate plays the curve forward then backward each cycle, so the return shows the same easing reversed
A delay before the first iteration is a pause before the loop starts; the spec wording points to a single initial wait, not a pause between loops
cm-css-loops.principle: A loop shows a curve's full path when each cycle plays it once in one direction and the reverse is visible.
signals: alternate on infinite loops
a delay that starts the loop only
cm-css-loops.note: Whether animation-delay repeats between iterations is an inference from the MDN wording (not stated directly on the fetched page).

cm-steps.text: steps() divides the transition into equal intervals and jumps between them instead of gliding. step-start is steps(1, start), which jumps to its end value at once. step-end is steps(1, end), which holds the start value and jumps at the finish. The page describes both as jumps rather than smooth transitions.

cm-velocity-ends.term: start and end velocity of a timing curve
cm-velocity-ends.text: The slope at the start of a cubic bezier timing curve is y1 over x1, and the slope at the end is (1 minus y2) over (1 minus x2). Those two slopes set how the motion begins and how it lands.
properties: slope is progress per unit of time
behaviors: A large y1 over a small x1 starts fast, so the first frames carry the most change
An x1 of 0 with y1 above 0 leaves the start vertical, a hard jump on the first frame
A small end slope lands gently and leaves a long tail
cm-velocity-ends.principle: The two ends of the curve carry the attack and the settle; the middle carries the travel.
signals: steep first ten percent of the curve reads as an attack
flat last ten percent reads as a settle

cm-numeric-check.term: numeric check of a timing curve
cm-numeric-check.text: Check a curve by sampling its parametric form: evaluate x(t) and y(t) for t from 0 to 1 using the bezier formulas, pair each x with its y to read progress over time, then confirm the end at t = 1 and record the largest y.
properties: parametric sample over t from 0 to 1
x(t) and y(t) built from P0 to P3
peak is the maximum of y(t)
behaviors: Dense samples reveal overshoot that a glance at the control points can miss
The sample at t = 1 returns (1, 1), which confirms the end point
Monotonicity is checked by seeing whether y(t) ever decreases after it starts rising
cm-numeric-check.principle: A curve can be checked before it runs, because every number it produces follows from its four control values.
signals: peak above 1 in the sample
settle time read where y stays within 1 percent of 1

cm-bezier-map.text: A cubic bezier timing function maps time (x, 0 to 1) to progress (y) along a curve from (0,0) to (1,1), set by two control points.
properties: two control points P1 and P2
behaviors: Steeper segments of the curve mean faster progress at that moment
A flat segment means the element holds near its current value
cm-bezier-map.principle: Progress over time is the whole feel of a motion; the curve is a picture of velocity.
signals: a curve rising steeply early reads as a fast attack
a long flat tail reads as a settle

cm-axes.term: x is time, y is progress

heading_path: What do the four numbers mean?

cm-axes.text: The four numbers are two control points, x1 y1 x2 y2; x is time and y is progress, and the page says y can run past the 0 to 1 band.
transfers: x sets the time fraction of the loop, y sets how far the element has travelled

cm-named-keywords.text: The CSS keywords are fixed control points: ease (0.25,0.1,0.25,1), ease-in (0.42,0,1,1), ease-out (0,0,0.58,1), ease-in-out (0.42,0,0.58,1); easings.net adds the Sine, Quad, Cubic, Quart, Quint, Expo, Circ, Back, Elastic and Bounce families.
behaviors: ease-out starts fast and lands slowly, so it reads as responsive on entry
ease-in starts slow and ends fast, so it reads as delayed on arrival
ease-in-out starts slow, moves fast in the middle, and arrives slow
ease-in holds back the start and ends with no deceleration, so the stop is abrupt
linear keeps a constant rate, the baseline the other curves bend away from
cm-named-keywords.principle: The keywords are a starting vocabulary; the family names describe how much the curve bends, not its feel on screen.
signals: a slow first 20 percent reads as a grip
a fast first 20 percent reads as an attack

cm-overshoot-numbers.text: With y2 above 1, cubic-bezier(0.34,1.56,0.64,1) peaks near 1.10 progress about 57 percent through its time and is back within 1 percent of the end by about 91 percent.
behaviors: Overshoot peak is set by y1 and y2 together, not by one control point alone
A bigger y2 raises the peak but lengthens the return
Peak timing moves with x1 and x2, so sampling the curve places the peak better than estimating it from the handles
cm-overshoot-numbers.principle: Overshoot is a number you can read off the control points, so a curve can be checked before it is run.
signals: peak progress 1.05 to 1.10 reads as a small kick
a peak near 1.1 with settle after 90 percent reads as a snap back

tokens.method_note: sampled numerically in this session from the bezier definition

heading_path: How do I make a bounce or overshoot?

cm-overshoot-from-y.text: Raising y1 above 1 pushes progress past the target early in the curve; raising y2 above 1 pushes it past the target later, near the end. The page's example cubic-bezier(.34, 1.56, .64, 1) has y1 at 1.56 and y2 at 1, so its overshoot comes from y1 and it peaks at 1.098 at x 0.573; it is an example, not a rule for every curve.
transfers: an overshoot kick can be tried by raising y1 and checking the dot's return, or by raising y2 for a kick later in the curve

cm-constraints.text: The spec limits only the x values of the control points to 0 through 1; the y values have no stated range, so the curve may leave the 0 to 1 band.
behaviors: A y value above 1 pushes progress past the target and creates overshoot
A negative y value pulls progress below the start before it rises
An x value outside 0 to 1 makes the curve invalid, so time would run backwards
cm-constraints.principle: Time has to move forward, so x is bounded; progress may overshoot, so y is free.
signals: cubic-bezier with x above 1 is rejected
y1 above 1 gives an early kick past the target
y2 above 1 gives a kick later, near the end

exemplars._about: Candidate pool, not a set. Each exemplar serves one or two readings of sticky or punchy; the consumer picks and composes. Values are candidates to check against a reading, not the deliverable.

ex-sticky-grip.text: The ease-in-out keyword holds the start back and releases in the middle, a grip-then-release shape from the spec's own keywords.
ex-sticky-grip.transfers: the slow first fifth that holds the element before it moves
ex-sticky-grip.does_not_transfer: the symmetric arrival; a grip without a settle can feel floaty

ex-sticky-early-settle.text: A strong ease-out reaches most of its travel early and holds near the end value, which reads as a settle and as a fast attack.
ex-sticky-early-settle.transfers: the early arrival and the long quiet tail near the target
ex-sticky-early-settle.does_not_transfer: a magnetic arrival; the tail is short and does not pull

ex-sticky-overshoot-snap.text: The Back easing family with the default overshoot constant 1.70158 peaks about 10 percent past the target near 58 percent of its time, then returns to 1.
ex-sticky-overshoot-snap.transfers: the past-the-target peak and the return to rest
ex-sticky-overshoot-snap.does_not_transfer: a hold at the end; the curve returns to 1 and stops, so the hold has to come from the pause after it

ex-sticky-magnetic.text: A strong ease-in-out moves fast through the middle and arrives slowly, which reads as being pulled onto a target.
ex-sticky-magnetic.transfers: a fast middle and a slow arrival at the target
ex-sticky-magnetic.does_not_transfer: a grip at the start; this curve starts from rest with less hold

ex-punchy-hard-stop.text: The easeOutExpo control points (0.16,1,0.3,1), named in search snippets and not fetched here, reach 90 percent progress by about 33 percent of the time and stop creeping by about 62 percent.
ex-punchy-hard-stop.transfers: the fast launch that makes the last movement look like a stop
ex-punchy-hard-stop.does_not_transfer: a settle that is long enough to read as grip; it is short and steep

serves: punchy: short duration with clear peak
ex-punchy-kick.text: cubic-bezier(0.34,1.56,0.64,1) peaks near 1.10 at about 57 percent of its time, a clear kick past the target that returns quickly at a short duration.
ex-punchy-kick.transfers: the single clear peak in the first half and the short return
ex-punchy-kick.does_not_transfer: a long wobble; the return is about a third of the duration

ex-punchy-fast-attack.text: Material's standard decelerate (0,0,0,1) starts at full speed and eases into rest, a fast attack that spends most of its time in the tail.
ex-punchy-fast-attack.does_not_transfer: a clear peak or kick; it has no overshoot

terms._about: Vocabulary for the timing curve and the two words.

terms-timing-vocab.text: Timing function, progress, control point, endpoint, overshoot and easing are the spec's terms for a bezier motion curve.

loop_presentation._about: Ways to show a timing curve as a loop: approaches with what each shows and hides, the loop's timing parameters with their status, and layouts for a set. Options, not a default presentation; each approach fits a different question.

options._about: options, not requirements: layouts for a set of three loops, each chosen by what the viewer should compare

lp-layout-options.term: layouts for a set of three loops
lp-layout-options.text: A set can sit in several layouts. Each one shows some differences and hides others.

options.option: stacked rows on a shared time axis
options.hides: each curve's shape on its own

options.option: one graph with three curves overlaid
three cards in a row, loops started together
one track with three dots staggered by start time

heading_path: How do I make a bounce or overshoot?

lp-overshoot-shown-by-dot.text: The page says an overshoot appears as the dot passing its end point and returning, so the preview is the check for overshoot.
transfers: a loop can make overshoot visible by letting the element run past its target and come back
lp-overshoot-shown-by-dot.interpretation: A loop that runs past the target and returns shows overshoot to a viewer without any numbers on screen.

lp-approach-bar-fill.text: A bar fills from empty toward a target mark, with fill length as progress. It reads as a meter, which suits a settle that holds near full.
behaviors: A plateau near the target shows the settle
A bar clamped at 100 percent hides any overshoot
shows: how far each curve has moved at a glance
hides: how the curve bends at its ends when clamped
lp-approach-bar-fill.fits_when: the viewer needs to compare progress across curves at one moment

lp-approach-graph-playhead.text: The curve is drawn on time and progress axes, and a vertical playhead sweeps across it. It shows the whole curve, including overshoot, settle and slope, but not what an element looks like moving.
behaviors: Slope at the playhead reads as velocity
The playhead crossing the peak marks the overshoot
shows: full curve with overshoot and settle
hides: the element as seen in context
lp-approach-graph-playhead.fits_when: the viewer needs the shape before the feel

lp-loop-timing.text: A loop should run long enough for the curve's settle to show. For the sample overshoot curve, progress is within 1 percent of the end by 91 percent of its duration, so a loop that ends at 100 percent shows the settle with room to spare.

tokens.reset: jump back to start, or an alternate pass

lp-frame-rate.text: Smoothness depends on the display refresh. Sixty frames per second is a common target, and higher refresh screens exist. No frame-rate source was gathered in this build, so treat the number as a starting point.

lp-dot-on-track.text: The editor previews the curve on a live element: a blue dot moves along a wide, empty horizontal track beneath the value field, so the eye reads timing as position over time.
lp-dot-on-track.visual_seen: Screenshot: one blue dot sits left of centre in a wide white track box; the track is otherwise empty; the CSS output box sits below.
transfers: one element driven by one curve, drawn on a plain track
a single shared track keeps the timing reading free of colour or scale cues
lp-dot-on-track.interpretation: The dot shows progress against time, not the curve's shape; a loop of this kind could show a moving element per curve on its own track. An overshoot would carry the dot past its end mark and back.
lp-dot-on-track.fits_when: the viewer needs to feel the travel as a moving object

lp-approach-css-element.term: CSS loop on the real element
lp-approach-css-element.text: The element runs the curve as a CSS animation with infinite iterations and alternate direction. It shows felt motion in context, and the curve only shows if a graph sits beside it.
behaviors: The return pass plays the same easing reversed, which may read differently from the forward pass
animation-delay waits before the first iteration; a rest between loops would need a hold in the keyframes instead
shows: the return pass as a reversed curve
lp-approach-css-element.fits_when: the viewer needs to judge the feel of the real interaction

quality_readings._about: Readings of the two quality words, side by side with no default. The pool holds exemplar curve shapes, each labeled with the reading it serves. The options area holds decisions that the readings raise. Inferred from the research shards 20 and 21; the consumer picks or combines.

pool._about: Candidate pool, not a set. Each exemplar serves the readings named in serves; the consumer samples one or two and composes. Values come from the research shards and are candidates to check against a reading, not the deliverable.

pool-ex-sticky-early-settle-punchy.text: Pool pointer to the exemplar ex-sticky-early-settle, serving the punchy reading; its values stay in exemplars.

pool-ex-sticky-overshoot-snap-punchy.text: Pool pointer to the exemplar ex-sticky-overshoot-snap, serving the punchy reading; its values stay in exemplars.

options._about: options, not requirements: decisions the readings raise, with the tradeoff of each. The dump does not answer them.

dp-combine.term: which sticky and which punchy reading share one curve
dp-combine.text: Pairing a sticky reading with a punchy reading in one curve either agrees, conflicts, or doubles up. Three pairings are open.
dp-combine.decision: which sticky reading and which punchy reading go into one curve

options.tradeoff: Both front-load velocity, so they agree. The curve gets speed and a settle, with no kick; it may read as a plain ease-out.
options.fits_when: the set should share one fast, planted feel

options.tradeoff: The kick and the snap-back are the same peak, so one curve is sticky and punchy at once. A deep peak reads as wobble, and the hold needs a pause after the return.
options.fits_when: the set should show one visible catch

options.tradeoff: They conflict: a grip holds back the start and a hard stop needs an early launch. The curve has to give up its first fifth or its last, and can read as two curves joined.
options.fits_when: the curves are meant to be compared, not blended

dp-curve-mapping.text: Each curve can carry one sticky reading, one punchy reading, both, or one reading shared across the curves. The choice is open.
dp-curve-mapping.decision: which sticky or punchy reading each curve carries

options.shows: holds, settles and catches, each on its own curve
options.tradeoff: no curve launches or kicks, so the punchy word goes unshown
options.fits_when: the viewer should see the sticky word on its own

options.shows: a fast attack, a kick or a hard stop, each on its own curve
options.tradeoff: no curve holds or settles, so the sticky word goes unshown
options.fits_when: the viewer should see the punchy word on its own

options.shows: a hold or settle followed by a launch or kick on the same curve
options.tradeoff: a grip and a hard stop conflict, and a deep peak reads as wobble
options.fits_when: one curve should carry both words at once

options.option: one reading shared across the curves
options.shows: one quality tuned at different intensities or durations
options.tradeoff: the two words are not told apart on screen
options.fits_when: the readings are meant to be compared as intensities of one quality

q-punchy.text: Punchy, as motion, has at least three readings: a fast attack, a short overshoot kick, and a hard stop. Punchy differs from fast: it needs a visible peak or a visible stop, not speed alone.

readings.in_practice: High velocity on the first frames, decelerating into rest. It reads as punchy when the first visible motion comes early; a fast curve with a long soft tail reads as merely fast.
signals: early speed peak
motion visible on the first frame
duration under about 300 ms

readings.in_practice: One clear peak past the target in the first half, then a quick return. A peak near 1.05 to 1.10 reads as a kick; a deeper peak or a long return reads as a wobble.
signals: single peak in the first half
peak about 1.05 to 1.10
return about a third of duration

readings.in_practice: A steep launch that flattens abruptly, so the last movement looks like a stop. Most of the progress arrives early and very little creeps in after.
signals: 90 percent of progress by about a third of time
near-zero speed for the final stretch

q-sticky.text: Sticky, as motion, has at least four readings: a grip before release, an early settle that holds, an overshoot that snaps back and holds, and a magnetic pull. Each gives a different curve, and none is the reading.

readings.in_practice: A slow first fifth holds the element before it moves, then the middle releases. The hold has to be visible, or the start reads as lag.
signals: slow first fifth of time
hold visible before motion
no overshoot

readings.in_practice: Most of the travel happens early, and the curve sits near the end value for a long quiet tail. The element looks planted before its duration ends.
signals: most progress before half of time
flat tail near 1
no return past 1

readings.reading: overshoot that snaps back and holds
readings.in_practice: The value passes the target by a small amount and returns to rest, so the element catches and then holds. Peak size and speed of return decide whether it reads as catch or as wobble.
signals: progress peaks above 1 mid-curve
return in the last third
pause or hold after the return

readings.in_practice: A fast middle and a slow arrival make the element look pulled onto its target. It has less grip at the start than the grip reading.
signals: fast middle of the curve
slow arrival at the target
little hold at the start

moodboard._about: Visual references for how a cubic-bezier motion curve is drawn: axes, endpoints, handles, the moving element, and the track. Six web images were collected (three static SVG graphs from the MDN easing reference, one MDN page capture, one LottieFiles easing-editor page capture, one Bushe cubic-bezier editor capture). Picks carry no license; treat each as a seed to look at and draw from, not as freely usable art. The two LottieFiles preset GIFs were blocked by robots rules and are not in the set.

mb-ease-family-graphs.term: CSS easing graphs: ease, ease-in, ease-out, ease-in-out as four small plots
signals: x axis labelled Input progress, y axis labelled Output progress, both running 0 to 1
dashed guides drawn from the curve endpoints to the top-right corner
blue stroke with a dot at each endpoint, curve starts at the origin and ends at (1,1)
control handles are not drawn; only the resulting curve and its endpoints are shown
ease-in stays low then rises steeply; ease-out rises early then flattens; ease-in-out is S-shaped

mb-linear-graph.term: linear easing graph: the constant-rate diagonal
signals: single straight blue line from (0,0) to (1,1) in a labelled square
tick marks at 0, 0.5, 1 on both axes, with dashed guides to the top-right corner
a plain diagonal reads as equal output change for every unit of input

mb-step-graphs.term: step-start and step-end graphs: stepped output with hard jumps
signals: two side-by-side square plots, each with a dashed guide line
horizontal blue runs with a single vertical jump, one jump at the start, one at the end
dots mark the open and closed ends of each step

mb-mdn-page-capture.term: MDN easing-function reference page, full-length capture
signals: a Values section with a labelled linear diagram, then keyword entries for ease, ease-in, ease-out, ease-in-out
the keyword graphs are too small in the capture to read, except the linear diagonal
a syntax block listing cubic-bezier(x1, y1, x2, y2) and steps(n, jump-start)
a long page at reduced scale; its value is the wording of the spec more than the pictures

mb-bushe-editor.term: CSS cubic-bezier editor: a live curve panel with a moving dot and copy-ready output
signals: numeric input for the four control values, shown as .25,.1,.25,1
a wide preview track in its own box, with a blue dot placed on the track as the moving element
a CSS output line below the preview: transition-timing-function: cubic-bezier(...)
a plain light panel with generous padding and a single blue accent

mb-lottie-editor-page.term: LottieFiles easing editor article: curve preview beside the feature image
signals: hero panel showing a dark easing-editor UI with a curve graph and numeric fields
two stacked phone-style frames contrasting animation without easing and with easing, read as a before and after of timing
section headings walk from base easings (linear, ease-in, ease-out, ease-in-out) to presets to custom bezier
preset GIFs were not captured in the page screenshot, so the preset curves are visible only in text

facets._about: What the images share when they draw a motion curve. Based on the six images above; the picks themselves carry no license.
facets.axes: Input progress runs along the horizontal axis and output progress along the vertical, both from 0 to 1. Dashed guides close the plot at the top and right. The static graphs put the curve in a square with tick marks at 0, 0.5 and 1.
facets.handles: The static MDN graphs show only the resulting curve and its endpoints; control handles are absent. The Bushe editor is the one image that makes the handles operable, as numeric fields that drive the curve.
facets.moving_element: A dot is the moving-element stand-in in these images: at the curve endpoints in the static graphs, and on the preview track in the Bushe editor. In both, the dot marks where the element sits on the curve.
facets.track: The static graphs have no time track. The Bushe editor draws a horizontal track where the dot travels, which is the closest image to a timeline. The LottieFiles page shows before and after frames rather than a track.
facets.shown_and_hidden: Shown: the curve, its endpoints, axis labels, and the copy-ready value. Hidden: control handles in the static graphs, any overshoot region above 1 or below 0 (the MDN graphs clip to the unit square), and any time scale in seconds.
facets.transfers: A loop presentation can reuse the labelled unit square with dashed guides and a single moving dot that travels the curve from start to end. Overshoot is not shown in any of these images, so a loop that goes past 1 on the output axis would extend the reference rather than copy it. The numeric-field and copy-ready readout of the Bushe editor transfers as a caption for each loop.
facets.limits: The palette is near-white with one blue accent in most of the images, so it transfers as a neutral frame rather than a colour direction. The LottieFiles preset GIFs were not collected, so no preset loop is described from them.

lexicon._about: Words for the feels, the curve and the loop: registers, associations, influences, search phrases and canonical terms. Brainstormed from the model's own knowledge; tier 3 and 4. Influence and association names are inferred, not checked against fetched pages here; the token values they point to live in curve_mechanics and task_discipline.

lx-reg-technical.text: Spec and tooling words that name the curve's parts and what they do to progress over time.
behaviors: A y control point above 1 lets progress pass the end value before returning
lx-reg-technical.principle: Technical words name where a shape lives on the curve, not how it feels.

lx-reg-perceptual.text: How the eye and hand read speed and weight across a motion.
behaviors: A fast first third reads as a snap; a slow middle reads as drag
signals: high velocity in the first frames
a long low-velocity stretch before rest
lx-reg-perceptual.principle: Perceived speed comes from where the velocity peaks, not from the total duration alone.

lx-reg-emotional.text: Mood words people use for a motion. They name a feeling, so they point toward a shape rather than name one.
behaviors: Firm and confident often come from a short arrival with little tail
lx-reg-emotional.principle: Mood words are a route into the curve's shape; pair each with a shape before using it.

lx-reg-practice.text: The words designers and engineers use for where a curve goes in an interface.
lx-reg-practice.principle: Practice words place a curve in a moment of the interaction, which is how the three curves can be told apart.

properties: the attack of a drum hit
behaviors: A short motion with a clear early peak reads as punchy even at a modest distance
lx-assoc-punchy.principle: Punchy is about the attack and the stop; the total length matters less than the first and last frames.

behaviors: A rest at each end of a loop lets a viewer see where the curve starts and where it finishes
lx-assoc-loops.principle: A repeating motion is read through its rests as much as its moves.

behaviors: A hand-tuned curve is judged against a reference motion the team already knows
lx-assoc-custom.principle: Custom values gain meaning when they are compared with a motion the reader already recognizes.

properties: a magnet pulling into a slot
behaviors: A slow start that grips, then releases, reads as sticky before the element arrives
Grip and catch describe the slow start, while plant and settle describe the arrival
lx-assoc-sticky.principle: Sticky is about how the motion holds to a point, so the middle and the arrival carry the feel.

contribution: an arrival with no visible bounce on large surfaces
lx-inf-ios-sheets.principle: Large surfaces read as heavy, so their arrival is quiet.

contribution: in, out and in-out variants of each family
lx-inf-penner.principle: Overshoot is a named family with its own in, out and in-out forms.

contribution: handles dragged on a speed graph, which trains the eye to shape speed over time rather than position
lx-inf-graph-editor.principle: A speed graph shows the curve as velocity, which is how sticky and punchy show up.

queries: easing curve that holds at the end
custom cubic bezier values for UI

lx-term-overshoot.text: Progress passes the end value and returns. Kick and wobble are informal names for small and large overshoot.

lx-term-loop-demo.text: A repeating animation that plays a curve on a track and resets. In this task, loops means repeat animation.
